Red-backed mousebirds (Colius colius) exhibit a suite of life-history traits that reflect their frugivorous diet and subtropical existence. The resting metabolic rate, measured through oxygen consumption during thermoneutral conditions, provides insight into their daily energetic requirements. Respirometry trials have revealed a maximum oxygen consumption of 32 milliliters per hour [JOi = 32 milliliters per hour] in the Red-backed mousebird, recorded when ambient temperatures reach 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] — a thermal condition that approximates the peak of a hot summer day in their native Karoo and fynbos habitats. This relatively elevated metabolic rate is consistent with values reported for other small-bodied mousebird species and reflects the high cost of sustaining resting energetic demands in a bird that frequently basks in direct sunlight to supplement its endogenous heat production. The oxygen demand at such high ambient temperatures is notable because the species must also dissipate heat effectively to avoid hyperthermia, a challenge met through behavioral mechanisms such as gular fluttering and postural adjustments that minimize heat gain. These metabolic measurements were obtained from post-absorptive, resting individuals during their inactive period, ensuring that the recorded values represent true basal conditions rather than the elevated rates associated with digestion or activity.

The reproductive strategy of the Red-backed mousebird is characterized by a modest output that aligns with its relatively slow life-history pace. Females typically produce between 1 and 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 8 eggs per clutch], with 1 to 3 clutches completed each year [F_R_i = 1 to 3 clutches completed each year], a pattern that is likely constrained by the seasonal availability of fleshy fruits, their primary food source. These values yield an overall annual reproductive rate of approximately 1 to 24 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 1 to 24 offspring per year], a pace that is low compared to many passerine species of similar body size, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes chick quality and parental care over high fecundity. The temperature conditions under which these reproductive rates were documented, approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], represent the typical ambient environment during the breeding season in the species' range. Field observations suggest that the timing of egg-laying is tightly synchronized with the peak fruiting period of keystone plant species such as the num-num (Carissa spp.) and various berry-producing shrubs, which provide the necessary energy for egg formation and subsequent chick provisioning.

Eggs of the Red-backed mousebird weigh 2.7 grams [Ww0 = 2.7 grams] at the time of laying, a modest initial investment that reflects the relatively small size of the egg relative to the female's body mass. This initial wet weight places the species among those with the smallest recorded egg mass within the Coliidae family, an observation that underscores the need for intensive maternal investment during the post-hatching period. The modest hatchling mass necessitates intensive brooding by both parents during the first several days post-hatching, as the altricial chicks are unable to thermoregulate independently. Growth during the initial nestling phase is remarkably rapid, with chicks more than doubling their mass within the first week as they receive frequent crop-milk-like regurgitations from both parents. The transition from complete dependency to the first successful flight marks a major developmental milestone in the species' life cycle.

A developmental sequence of key life-history events unfolds under the warm thermal conditions typical of the breeding season in southern Africa. When incubating eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], the incubation period lasts approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days], a duration that is consistent with the prolonged embryonic development observed in other frugivorous birds. This incubation period, established from observations of the congener Colius castanotus, suggests that embryonic development in the Red-backed mousebird proceeds at a moderate pace, likely constrained by the relatively large egg size relative to the mother's body mass. After hatching, the nestlings progress through a series of feather-development stages, with the first successful flight — fledging — occurring 11 days after hatching [tx = 11 days after hatching] when ambient temperatures reach 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This rapid fledging period is short compared to many other altricial species and may represent an adaptive response to high predation pressure in their open scrubland habitats. The post-fledging period involves continued parental provisioning as the young birds develop their flight capabilities and foraging skills.

Sexual maturation in the Red-backed mousebird occurs relatively early in life, with individuals reaching puberty at 33 days after hatching [tp = 33 days after hatching] under the warm ambient conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This rapid attainment of reproductive maturity is typical of small-bodied birds that face high annual mortality rates and must reproduce quickly to maintain population numbers. However, despite reaching physiological puberty early, individuals typically defer their first breeding attempt until they are approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching], a delay that likely reflects the need to acquire breeding territories and develop the social bonds required for successful at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]pair formation. The maximum recorded longevity for the species in the wild is approximately 11.5 years [am = approximately 11.5 years] when measured under the same thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a lifespan that is notably long for a bird of its small body size. This extended longevity positions the Red-backed mousebird as a classic slow life-history strategist within the avian community, a pattern that is reinforced by its stable, predictable food supply and relatively low extrinsic mortality from predation in its scrubland environment. Adult females ultimately reach a maximum body mass of 45 grams [Wwi = 45 grams], a value that represents the upper end of the size range for females in this species and reflects the accumulation of body reserves necessary to support the energetic costs of egg production and incubation.
